newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - HK Chinese to profit from homes in London.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK Chinese to profit from homes in London.

text.p: Hong Kong Chinese have been furiously buying homes in prestigious parts of London ahead of the return of the British colony to China, driving prices sky-high.
Along with buyers from Asian Tiger economies such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, the Hong Kong Chinese have snapped up the lion's share of the top end of the London housing market.
But the exodus of capital from Hong Kong has not been prompted by fear ahead of the handover, analysts say. The Hong Kong Chinese are being lured by the returns the London property market offers.
"Buying a bolt-hole is just part of it," said Geoff Marsh of London Residential Research.
"Hong Kong Chinese are now buying into the London property market for strategic investment reasons. They're buying the properties to rent them out."
Despite a boom in London house prices, a house in Hong Kong still costs around double its London equivalent.
Renting out a London apartment yields a return of between eight and nine percent, a far cry from the three to four percent Hong Kong offers.
The gap is widening. Hong Kong's housing market is booming, with estate agent statistics showing property prices rising between 20 to 30 percent each year.

Vancouver, in the Canadian province of British Colombia, once the prime residential investment market for the overseas Chinese community, and the second most popular property investment market after London, no longer offers the competitive returns of the early 1990s.
LONDON LUXURY PROPERTY BECOMING SCARCE
But despite a boom that has seen house prices in some parts of London double over the past year, property at the luxury end is now becoming scarce, analysts say.
Estate agents estimate that during the next 10 years London will require another 100,000 apartments to cater for an influx of overseas executives posted to the capital.
As a result overseas investors are starting to consider purchasing commercial office buildings with a view to converting them to residential accommodation.

Commercial to residential conversions offer high returns. Central London freehold office property sells at around 125 pounds ($204) sterling per square foot (0.09 square metres). Residential property at the top end goes for around 325 pounds.
Asian buyers have left their most resounding mark on the luxury end of the London property market, analysts say.

In the affluent West End boroughs of Westminster and Kensington, as much as 60 percent of newly-developed prime residential properties have been snapped up by private Far Eastern investors over the past 24 months, according to Pierre Rolin, head of international real estate at Credit Suisse Private Banking.
"They are diversifying their investments," Rolin said. "Real estate is now regarded as a credible global asset."
BUYING SIGHT AND SITE UNSEEN
Far Eastern private investors at the top end of the market are buying entire newly developed blocks of around 50 apartments in the British capital.
And because of the potential profits to be made, and their links to the vast Chinese network in London, they are ready to buy the developments unseen, Rolin said.
"A lot of prime location residential purchases are not just being bought unseen. They're being bought off-plan. There's no building yet," he added.
"Asian investors have connections through the overseas Chinese network. The Chinese based in London are part of the infrastructure which helps the overseas invest here."
The trend to buy unseen has percolated through to smaller investors from the region who are also prepared to buy before viewing. Some analysts said these amateur investors could get burnt.

"Because they're just looking for the returns London offers, Hong Kong Chinese investors are buying London properties from Hong Kong without even seeing where they are located," said Stewart Morley, head of research at international property advisors Grimley.
"I would have thought it was dangerous for them not to know the state of the property cycle here, let alone not knowing the the value of the building at the time."
